processing: Fully oxidised: fresh Xinyang leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, in a process developed for the local green tea leaf.
harvest_season: The tea was created to make use of summer and autumn leaf that Xinyang's green tea trade valued less; finer grades use young, tippy leaf.
appearance_dry: Fine, tight strands in dark brown to near-black, with golden tips in the better grades.
appearance_liquor: Clear bright red, with a golden ring at the edge of the cup in good examples.
appearance_wet: Tender, even leaf in a bright red-brown.
taste_profile: Sweet and mellow with a clean finish; producers describe the aroma as chestnut joined with osmanthus.

brewing.notes: Slightly cooler water suits the tippy top grades. Lower grades take water just off the boil and a mug-style steep.

vintage_note: A young category, sold since about 2010 as current-year tea and graded rather than sold by vintage. As with other Chinese gongfu blacks, drink it within a year or two for the freshest aroma. The grades run from top grade through first and second, so ask which one you are buying.
description:
Xinyang is green tea country, the home of Xinyang Maojian, so a black tea from the same hills is a surprise. Xinyang Hong is that surprise: a northern Chinese black tea from southern Henan, made from local leaf and sold under its own protected trademark.

The idea was practical. Green tea earns its money in spring, and later leaf sold for little, so the region tried turning it into black tea instead. The leaf goes through withering, rolling, oxidation and drying, which turns the sharper summer character into something rounder.

In the cup, expect a bright red liquor and a sweet, mellow, clean taste. Local descriptions settle on chestnut and osmanthus, which is a fair thing to look for, though treat it as a house description more than a guarantee. Gaiwan steeps keep it lively, and long steeps in a mug work for the plainer grades.

The grades are defined by tightness, golden tips and aroma: top grade is fine and tippy with a tender sweet scent, while second grade shows some stem and fewer tips. Because the tea is new, there is no aged market to speak of, so buy recent stock.
history:
Unlike most Chinese regional teas, this one has a clear birth date. In late December 2009, during an inspection visit to Xinyang, the official Lu Zhangong urged the region to pick more summer and autumn leaf and to try black tea, and gave it the name Xinyang Hong. It reached the market from 2010.

A geographical certification trademark for Xinyang Hong was registered in 2013, and a trade standard for the tea, GH/T 1248-2019, followed.
